title: Essex named UK's third biggest haunted road hotspot with 50 reports
excerpt: Essex is named the UK's third-biggest haunted road hotspot, with 50 paranormal reports, including ghostly sightings near Colchester and Margaretting.
content:
Essex has been named one of the UK's biggest haunted road hotspots after 50 paranormal reports were linked to roads across the county.

The county ranked third nationally in research released ahead of Halloween by used car retailer Cinch, which analysed more than 1,100 reports listed in The Paranormal Database's Roads & Motorways section.

Only Wiltshire, with 57 reports, and Dorset, with 51, ranked higher than Essex in the study.

Essex also topped the list for the highest number of haunted road reports submitted directly by members of the public, with 21 sightings.

Among the accounts is a 2023 report near Margaretting, where a driver described seeing what appeared to be a fast-moving, legless figure crossing the road in front of their car before disappearing over a ditch.

In Colchester, a driver travelling along Maldon Road reported seeing a strange white triangle in 2023.

Another account from Mersea Road describes a driver spotting a teenage boy sitting in the back seat through their rear-view mirror, only for the seat to appear empty when they turned around.

Elsewhere in Essex, a motorist travelling near Little Hallingbury reportedly encountered a floating black figure in the road, forcing them to brake.

A separate report near North Shoebury describes a driver swerving after a man appeared from a hedge before seemingly disappearing.

The Paranormal Database combines reports from members of the public with accounts drawn from published media, historical records and other sources.

The wider East of England ranked second among English regions, with 187 haunted road reports, behind the South West with 218.

Essex, Suffolk and Norfolk accounted for 134 reports between them, with Suffolk recording 45 and Norfolk 39.

Ben Welham, motoring expert at Cinch, said: "Whether you believe in ghosts or not, seeing something you can't explain while you're driving would be enough to catch anyone off guard.

"Some of the stories have been around for decades, while others have been submitted much more recently, so it's clear they still capture people's imagination.

"It'll be interesting to see if any new sightings are reported this Halloween."

He also reminded motorists that darker evenings can make shapes and movement harder to judge, particularly on rural or unfamiliar roads, stressing the importance of leaving enough time and space to react safely.
